entries.22ce8194e690ee337c21bc0c8de4e60c5e9548d7: <div sID="gen2061" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="32" osisID="Exod.32" sID="Exod.32"/> <div eID="gen2061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2062" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2063" type="x-p"/> It is a very lamentable interruption which the story of this chapter gives to the record of the establishment of the church, and of religion among the Jews. Things went on admirably well towards that happy settlement: God had shown himself very favourable, and the people also had seemed to be pretty tractable. Moses had now almost completed his forty days upon the mount, and, we may suppose, was pleasing himself with the thoughts of the very joyful welcome he should have to the camp of Israel at his return, and the speedy setting up of the tabernacle among them. But, behold, the measures are broken, the sin of Israel turns away those good things from them, and puts a stop to the current of God's favours; the sin that did the mischief (would you think it?) was worshipping a golden calf. The marriage was ready to be solemnized between God and Israel, but Israel plays the harlot, and so the match is broken, and it will be no easy matter to piece it again. Here is, I. The sin of Israel, and of Aaron particularly, in making the golden calf for a god (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.1-Exod.32.4">ver. 1-4</reference>), and worshipping it, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.5-Exod.32.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. II. The notice which God gave of this to Moses, who was now in the mount with him, (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.7-Exod.32.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>), and the sentence of his wrath against them, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.9-Exod.32.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. III. The intercession which Moses immediately made for them in the mount (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.11-Exod.32.13">ver. 11-13</reference>), and the prevalency of that intercession, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.14">ver. 14</reference>. IV. His coming down from the mount, when he became an eye-witness of their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.15-Exod.32.19">ver. 15-19</reference>), in abhorrence of which, and as an expression of just indignation, he broke the tables (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.19">ver. 19</reference>), and burnt the golden calf, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.20">ver. 20</reference>. V. The examination of Aaron about it, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.21-Exod.32.24">ver. 21-24</reference>. VI. Execution done upon the ring-leaders in the idolatry, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.25-Exod.32.29">ver. 25-29</reference>. VII. The further intercession Moses made for them, to turn away the wrath of God from them (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.30-Exod.32.32">ver. 30-32</reference>), and a reprieve granted thereupon, reserving them for a further reckoning, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.33-Exod.32.35">ver. 33</reference>, &c.
entries.6d15a0adf029f8b90fe1c1df605c51068796ae15: <div eID="gen2063" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2062" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Golden Calf. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2064" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron, and said unto him, Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for <hi type="italic">as for</hi> this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Aaron said unto them, Break off the golden earrings, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the ears of your wives, of your sons, and of your daughters, and bring <hi type="italic">them</hi> unto me. <hi type="super">3</hi> And all the people brake off the golden earrings which <hi type="italic">were</hi> in their ears, and brought <hi type="italic">them</hi> unto Aaron. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he received <hi type="italic">them</hi> at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These <hi type="italic">be</hi> thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt. 5 And when Aaron saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he built an altar before it; and Aaron made proclamation, and said, To morrow <hi type="italic">is</hi> a feast to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> And they rose up early on the morrow, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play. <div eID="gen2064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2065" type="x-p"/> While Moses was in the mount, receiving the law from God, the people had time to meditate upon what had been delivered, and prepare themselves for what was further to be revealed, and forty days was little enough for that work; but, instead of that, there were those among them that were contriving how to break the laws they had already received, and to anticipate those which they were in expectation of. On the thirty-ninth day of the forty, the plot broke out of rebellion against the Lord. Here is, <div eID="gen2065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2066" type="x-p"/> I. A tumultuous address which the people made to Aaron, who was entrusted with the government in the absence of Moses: <hi type="italic">Up, make us gods, which shall go before us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.1">v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen2066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2067" type="x-p"/> 1. See the ill effect of Moses's absence from them; if he had not had God's call both to go and stay, he would not have been altogether free from blame. Those that have the charge of others, as magistrates, ministers, and masters of families, ought not, without just cause, to absent themselves from their charge, <hi type="italic">lest Satan get advantage</hi> thereby. <div eID="gen2067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2068" type="x-p"/> 2. See the fury and violence of a multitude when they are influenced and corrupted by such as lie in wait to deceive. Some few, it is likely, were at first possessed with this humour, while many, who would never have thought of it if they had not put it into their hearts, were brought to follow their pernicious ways; and presently such a multitude were carried down the stream that the few who abhorred the proposal durst not so much as enter their protestation against it. <hi type="italic">Behold how great a matter a little fire kindles!</hi> Now what was the matter with this giddy multitude? <div eID="gen2068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2069" type="x-p"/> (1.) They were weary of waiting for the promised land. They thought themselves detained too long at mount Sinai; though there they lay very safe and very easy, well fed and well taught, yet they were impatient to be going forward. They had a God that staid with them, and manifested his presence with them by the cloud; but this would not serve. They must have a god to go before them; they are for hastening to the land <hi type="italic">flowing with milk and honey,</hi> and cannot stay to take their religion along with them. Note, Those that would anticipate God's counsels are commonly precipitate in their own. We must first wait for God's law before we catch at his promises. He that believeth doth not make haste, not more haste than good speed. <div eID="gen2069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2070" type="x-p"/> (2.) They were weary of waiting for the return of Moses. When he went up into the mount, he had not told them (for God had not told him) how long he must stay; and therefore, when he had outstayed their time, though they were every way well provided for in his absence, some bad people advanced I know not what surmises concerning his delay: <hi type="italic">As for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of Egypt, we wot not what has become of him.</hi> Observe, [1.] How slightly they speak of his person—<hi type="italic">this Moses.</hi> Thus ungrateful are they to Moses, who had shown such a tender concern for them, and thus do they walk contrary to God. While God delights to put honour upon him, they delight to put contempt upon him, and this to the face of Aaron his brother, and now his viceroy. Note, The greatest merits cannot secure men from the greatest indignities and affronts in this ungrateful world. [2.] How suspiciously they speak of his delay: <hi type="italic">We wot not what has become of him.</hi> They thought he was either consumed by the devouring fire or starved for want to food, as if that God who kept and fed them, who were so unworthy, would not take care for the protection and supply of Moses his favourite. Some of them, who were willing to think well of Moses, perhaps suggested that he was translated to heaven like Enoch; while others that cared not how ill they thought of him insinuated that he had deserted his undertaking, as unable to go on with it, and had returned to his father-in-law to keep his flock. All these suggestions were perfectly groundless and absurd, nothing could be more so; it was easy to tell <hi type="italic">what had become of him:</hi> he was seen to go into the cloud, and the cloud he went into was still seen by all Israel upon the top of the mount; they had all the reason in the world to conclude that he was safe there; if the Lord had been pleased to kill him, he would not have shown him such favours as these. If he tarried long, it was because God had a great deal to say to him, for their good; he resided upon the mount as the ambassador, and he would certainly return as soon as he had finished the business he went upon; and yet they make this the colour for their wicked proposal: <hi type="italic">We wot not what has become of him.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Those that are resolved to think ill, when they have ever so much reason to think well, commonly pretend that they know not what to think. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Misinterpretations of our Redeemer's delays are the occasion of a great deal of wickedness. Our Lord Jesus has gone up into the mount of glory, where he is appearing in the presence of Gold for us, but out of our sight; the heavens must contain him, must conceal him, that we may live by faith. There he has been long; there he is yet. Hence unbelievers suggest that they know not what has become of him; and ask, <hi type="italic">Where is the promise of his coming?</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2 Pet. iii. 4</reference>), as if, because he has not come yet, he would never come. The wicked servant emboldens himself in his impieties with this consideration, <hi type="italic">My Lord delays his coming. Thirdly,</hi> Weariness in waiting betrays us to a great many temptations. This began Saul's ruin; he staid for Samuel to the last hour of the time appointed, but had not patience to stay that hour (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.8">1 Sam. xiii. 8</reference>, &c.); so Israel here, if they could but have staid one day longer, would have seen what had become of Moses. <hi type="italic">The Lord is a God of judgment,</hi> and must be waited for till he comes waited for though he tarry; and then we shall not lose our labour, for he that shall come will come, and will not tarry. <div eID="gen2070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2071" type="x-p"/> (3.) They were weary of waiting for a divine institution of religious worship among them for that was the thing they were now in expectation of. They were told that they must <hi type="italic">serve God in this mountain,</hi> and fond enough they would be of the pomp and ceremony of it; but, because that was not appointed them so soon as they wished, they would set their own wits on work to devise signs of God's presence with them, and would glory in them, and have a worship of their own invention, probably such as they had seen among the Egyptians; for Stephen says that when they said unto Aaron, <hi type="italic">Make us gods,</hi> they did, in heart, <hi type="italic">turn back into Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.7.39-Acts.7.40">Acts vii. 39, 40</reference>. This was a very strange motion, <hi type="italic">Up, make us gods.</hi> If they knew not what had become of Moses, and thought him lost, it would have been decent for them to have appointed a solemn mourning for him for certain days; but see how soon so great a benefactor is forgotten. If they had said, "Moses is lost, make us a governor," there would have been some sense in it, though a great deal of ingratitude to the memory of Moses, and contempt of Aaron and Hur who were left lords-justices in his absence; but to say, <hi type="italic">Moses is lost, make us a god,</hi> was the greatest absurdity imaginable. Was Moses their god? Had he ever pretended to be so? Whatever had become of Moses, was it not evident, beyond contradiction that God was still with them? And had they any room to question his leading their camp who victualled it so well every day? Could they have any other god that would provide so well for them as he had done, nay as he now did? And yet, <hi type="italic">Make us gods, which shall go before us! Gods!</hi> How many would they have? Is not one sufficient? <hi type="italic">Make us gods!</hi> and what good would gods of their own making do them? They must have such gods to go before them as could not go themselves further than they were carried. So wretchedly besotted and intoxicated are idolaters: they are <hi type="italic">mad upon their idols,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jer. l. 38</reference>. <div eID="gen2071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2072" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the demand which Aaron makes of their jewels thereupon: <hi type="italic">Bring me your golden ear-rings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.2">v. 2</reference>. We do not find that he said one word to discountenance their proposal; he did not reprove their insolence, did not reason with them to convince them of the sin and folly of it, but seemed to approve the motion, and showed himself not unwilling to humour them in it. One would hope he designed, at first, only to make a jest of it, and, by setting up a ridiculous image among them, to expose the motion, and show them the folly of it. But, if so, it proved ill jesting with sin: it is of dangerous consequence for the unwary fly to play about the candle. Some charitably suppose that when Aaron told them to break off their ear-rings, and bring them to him, he did it with design to crush the proposal, believing that though their covetousness would have let them <hi type="italic">lavish gold out of the bag</hi> to make an idol of (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.6">Isa. xlvi. 6</reference>), yet their pride would not have suffered them to part with the golden ear-rings. But it is not safe to try how far men's sinful lusts will carry them in a sinful way, and what expense they will be at; it proved here a dangerous experiment. <div eID="gen2072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2073" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the making of the golden calf, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.3-Exod.32.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. 1. The people brought in their ear-rings to Aaron, whose demand of them, instead of discouraging the motion, perhaps did rather gratify their superstition, and beget in them a fancy that the gold taken from their ears would be the most acceptable, and would make the most valuable god. Let their readiness to part with their rings to make an idol of shame us out of our niggardliness in the service of the true God. Did they not draw back from the charge of their idolatry? And shall we grudge the expenses of our religion, or starve so good a cause? 2. Aaron melted down their rings, and, having a mould prepared for the purpose, poured the melted gold into it, and then produced it in the shape of an ox or calf, giving it some finishing strokes with a graving tool. Some think that Aaron chose this figure, for a sign or token of the divine presence, because he thought the head and horns of an ox a proper emblem of the divine power, and yet, being so plain and common a thing, he hoped the people would not be so sottish as to worship it. But it is probable that they had learnt of the Egyptians thus to represent the Deity, for it is said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.8">Ezek. xx. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">They did not forsake the idols of Egypt,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.8">ch. xxiii. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Neither left she her whoredoms brought from Egypt. Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.20">Ps. cvi. 20</reference>), and proclaimed their own folly, beyond that of other idolaters, who worshipped the host of heaven. <div eID="gen2073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2074" type="x-p"/> IV. Having made the calf in Horeb, they <hi type="italic">worshipped the graven image,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.106.19">Ps. cvi. 19</reference>. Aaron, seeing the people fond of their calf, was willing yet further to humour them, and he built an altar before it, and proclaimed a feast to the honour of it (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.5">v. 5</reference>), a feast of dedication. Yet he calls it <hi type="italic">a feast to Jehovah;</hi> for, brutish as they were, they did not imagine that this image was itself a god, nor did they design to terminate their adoration in the image, but they made it for a representation of the true God, whom they intended to worship in and through this image; and yet this did not excuse them from gross idolatry, any more than it will excuse the papists, whose plea it is that they do not worship the image, but God by the image, so making themselves just such idolaters as the worshippers of the golden calf, whose feast was a feast to Jehovah, and proclaimed to be so, that the most ignorant and unthinking might not mistake it. The people are forward enough to celebrate this feast (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">They rose up early on the morrow,</hi> to show how well pleased they were with the solemnity, and, according to the ancient rites of worship, they offered sacrifice to this new-made deity, and then feasted upon the sacrifice; thus having, at the expense of their ear-rings, made their god, they endeavour, at the expense of their beasts, to make this god propitious. Had they offered these sacrifices immediately to Jehovah, without the intervention of an image, they might (for aught I know) have been accepted (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.24">ch. xx. 24</reference>); but having set up an image before them as a symbol of God's presence, and so changed the truth of God into a lie, these sacrifices were an abomination, nothing could be more so. When the idolatry of theirs is spoken of in the New Testament the account of their feast upon the sacrifice is quoted and referred to (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.7">1 Cor. x. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They sat down to eat and drink</hi> of the remainder of what was sacrificed, and then <hi type="italic">rose up to play,</hi> to play the fool, to play the wanton. Like god, like worship. They would not have made a calf their god if they had not first made their belly their god; but, when the god was a jest, no marvel that the service was sport. Being <hi type="italic">vain in their imaginations,</hi> they became vain in their worship, so great was this vanity. Now, 1. It was strange that any of the people, especially so great a number of them, should do such a thing. Had they not, but the other day, in this very place, heard the voice of the Lord God speaking to them out of the midst of the fire, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not make to thyself any graven image?</hi> Had they not heard the thunder, seen the lightnings, and felt the earthquake, with the dreadful pomp of which this law was given? Had they not been particularly cautioned not to make <hi type="italic">gods of gold?</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.20.23">ch. xx. 23</reference>. Nay, had they not themselves solemnly entered into covenant with God, and promised that all that which he had said unto them they <hi type="italic">would do, and would be obedient?</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.24.7">ch. xxiv. 7</reference>. And yet, before they stirred from the place where this covenant had been solemnly ratified, and before the cloud was removed from the top of Mount Sinai, thus to break an express command, in defiance of an express threatening that this <hi type="italic">iniquity should be visited upon them and their children</hi>—what shall be think of it? It is a plain indication that the law was no more able to sanctify than it was to justify; by it is the knowledge of sin, but not the cure of it. This is intimated in the emphasis laid upon the place where this sin was committed (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.19">Ps. cvi. 19</reference>). <hi type="italic">They made a calf in Horeb,</hi> the very place where the law was given. It was otherwise with those that received the gospel; they immediately <hi type="italic">turned from idols;</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1 Thess. i. 9</reference>. 2. It was especially strange that Aaron should be so deeply implicated in this sin, that he should make the calf, and proclaim the feast! Is this Aaron, the saint of the Lord, the brother of Moses his prophet, that could <hi type="italic">speak so well.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.14">ch. iv. 14</reference>), and yet speaks not one word against this idolatry? Is this he that had not only seen, but had been employed in summoning, the plagues of Egypt, and the judgments, executed upon the gods of the Egyptians? What! and yet himself copying out the abandoned idolatries of Egypt? With what face could they say, <hi type="italic">These are thy gods</hi> that <hi type="italic">brought thee out of Egypt,</hi> when they thus bring the idolatry of Egypt (the worst thing there) along with them? Is this Aaron, who had been with Moses in the mount (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.24">ch. xix. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.24.9">xxiv. 9</reference>), and knew that there was no manner of similitude seen there, by which they might make an image? Is this Aaron who was entrusted with the care of the people in the absence of Moses? Is he aiding and abetting in this rebellion against the Lord? How was it possible that he should ever do so sinful a thing? Either he was strangely surprised into it, and did it when he was half asleep, or he was frightened into it by the outrages of the rabble. The Jews have a tradition that his colleague Hur opposing it the people fell upon him and stoned him (and therefore we never read of him after) and that this frightened Aaron into a compliance. And God left him to himself, [1.] To teach us what the best of men are when they are so left, that we may <hi type="italic">cease from man,</hi> and that he who <hi type="italic">thinks he stands may take heed lest he fall.</hi> [2.] Aaron was, at this time, destined by the divine appointment to the great office of the priesthood; though he knew it not, Moses in the mount did. Now, lest he should be <hi type="italic">lifted up, above measure,</hi> with the honours that were to be put upon him, a messenger of Satan was suffered to prevail over him, that the remembrance thereof might keep him humble all his days. He who had once shamed himself so far as to build an altar to a golden calf must own himself altogether unworthy of the honour of attending at the altar of God, and purely indebted to free grace for it. Thus pride and boasting were for ever silenced, and a good effect brought out of a bad cause. By this likewise it was shown that <hi type="italic">the law made those priests who had infirmity, and needed first to offer for their own sins.</hi>
entries.85e5ab8c984ddb29240a1503085e5bce9c7433b8: <div eID="gen2074" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Intercession of Moses. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2075" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Go, get thee down; for thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted <hi type="italic">themselves:</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> They have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them: they have made them a molten calf, and have worshipped it, and have sacrificed thereunto, and said, These <hi type="italic">be</hi> thy gods, O Israel, which have brought thee up out of the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, I have seen this people, and, behold, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a stiffnecked people: <hi type="super">10</hi> Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation. 11 And Moses besought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God, and said, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , why doth thy wrath wax hot against thy people, which thou hast brought forth out of the land of Egypt with great power, and with a mighty hand? <hi type="super">12</hi> Wherefore should the Egyptians speak, and say, For mischief did he bring them out, to slay them in the mountains, and to consume them from the face of the earth? Turn from thy fierce wrath, and repent of this evil against thy people. <hi type="super">13</hi> Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, thy servants, to whom thou swarest by thine own self, and saidst unto them, I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have spoken of will I give unto your seed, and they shall inherit <hi type="italic">it</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> repented of the evil which he thought to do unto his people. <div eID="gen2075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2076" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God acquaints Moses with what was doing in the camp while he was absent, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.7-Exod.32.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. He could have told him sooner, as soon as the first step was taken towards it, and have hastened him down to prevent it; but he suffered it to come to this height, for wise and holy ends, and then sent him down to punish it. Note, It is no reproach to the holiness of God that he suffers sin to be committed, since he knows, not only how to restrain it when he pleases, but how to make it serviceable to the designs of his own glory. Observe what God here says to Moses concerning this sin. 1. That they had <hi type="italic">corrupted themselves.</hi> Sin is the corruption or depravation of the sinner, and it is a self-corruption; <hi type="italic">every man is tempted when he is drawn aside of his own lust.</hi> 2. That they had <hi type="italic">turned aside out of the way.</hi> Sin is a deviation from the way of our duty into a by-path. When they promised to do all that God should command them, they set out as fair as could be; but now they missed their way, and turned aside. 3. That they had turned aside quickly, quickly after the law was given them and they had promised to obey it, quickly after God had done such great things for them and declared his kind intentions to do greater. <hi type="italic">They soon forgot his works.</hi> To fall into sin quickly after we have renewed our covenants with God, or received special mercy from him, is very provoking. 4. He tells him particularly what they had done: <hi type="italic">They have made a calf, and worshipped it.</hi> Note, Those sins which are concealed from our governors are naked and open before God. He sees that which they cannot discover, nor is any of the wickedness in the world hidden from him. We could not bear to see the thousandth part of that provocation which God sees every day and yet keeps silence. 5. He seems to disown them, in saying to Moses, They are <hi type="italic">thy people whom thou broughtest up out of the land of Egypt;</hi> as if he had said, "I will not own any relation to them, or concern for them; let it never be said that they are my people, or that I brought them out of Egypt." Note, Those that corrupt themselves not only shame themselves, but even make God himself ashamed of them and of his kindness to them. 6. He sends him down to them with all speed: <hi type="italic">Go, get thee down.</hi> He must break off even his communion with God to go and do his duty as a magistrate among the people; so must Joshua, <reference osisRef="Exod.7.10">ch. vii. 10</reference>. Every thing is beautiful in its season. <div eID="gen2076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2077" type="x-p"/> II. He expresses his displeasure against Israel for this sin, and the determination of his justice to cut them off, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.9-Exod.32.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. 1. He gives this people their true character: "<hi type="italic">It is a stiff-necked people,</hi> unapt to come under the yoke of the divine law, and governed as it were by a spirit of contradiction, averse to all good and prone to evil, obstinate against the methods employed for their cure." Note, The righteous God sees, not only what we do, but what we are, not only the actions of our lives, but the dispositions of our spirits, and has an eye to them in all his proceedings. 2. He declares what was their just desert—that his wrath should <hi type="italic">wax hot against them,</hi> so as to consume them at once, and <hi type="italic">blot out their name from under heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.14">Deut. ix. 14</reference>); not only cast them out of covenant, but chase them out of the world. Note, Sin exposes us to the wrath of God; and that wrath, if it be not allayed by divine mercy, will burn us up as stubble. It were just with God to let the law have its course against sinners, and to cut them off immediately in the very act of sin; and, if he should do so, it would be neither loss nor dishonour to him. 3. He holds out inducements to Moses not to intercede for them: <hi type="italic">Therefore, let me alone.</hi> What did Moses, or what could he do, to hinder God from consuming them? When God resolves to abandon a people, and the decree of ruin has gone forth, no intercession can prevent it, <reference osisRef="Eze.14.14">Ezek. xiv. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="15.1">Jer. xv. 1</reference>. But God would thus express the greatness of his just displeasure against them, after the manner of men, who would have none to intercede for those they resolve to be severe with. Thus also he would put an honour upon prayer, intimating that nothing but the intercession of Moses could save them from ruin, that he might be a type of Christ, by whose mediation alone God would <hi type="italic">reconcile the world unto himself.</hi> That the intercession of Moses might appear the more illustrious, God fairly offers him that, if he would not interpose in this matter, he would <hi type="italic">make of him a great nation,</hi> that either, in process of time, he would raise up a people out of his loins, or that he would immediately, by some means or other, bring another great nation under his government and conduct, so that he should be no loser by their ruin. Had Moses been of a narrow selfish spirit, he would have closed with this offer; but he prefers the salvation of Israel before the advancement of his own family. Here was a man fit to be a governor. <div eID="gen2077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2078" type="x-p"/> III. Moses earnestly intercedes with God on their behalf (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.11-Exod.32.13">v. 11-13</reference>): he besought the Lord his God. If God would not be called <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> yet he hoped he might address him as <hi type="italic">his own God.</hi> What interest we have at the throne of grace we should improve for the church of God, and for our friends. Now Moses is standing in the gap to turn away the wrath of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Ps. cvi. 23</reference>. He wisely took the hint which God gave him when he said, <hi type="italic">Let me alone,</hi> which, though it seemed to forbid his interceding, did really encourage it, by showing what power the prayer of faith has with God. In such a case, God <hi type="italic">wonders if there be no intercessor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Isa. lix. 16</reference>. Observe, 1. His prayer (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Turn from thy fierce wrath;</hi> not as if he thought God was not justly angry, but he begs that he would not be so greatly angry as to consume them. "Let mercy rejoice against judgment; <hi type="italic">repent of this evil;</hi> change the sentence of destruction into that of correction." 2. His pleas. He fills his mouth with arguments, not to move God, but to express his own faith and to excite his own fervency in prayer. He urges, (1.) God's interest in them, the great things he had already done for them, and the vast expense of favours and miracles he had been at upon them, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.11">v. 11</reference>. God had said to Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.7">v. 7</reference>), They are <hi type="italic">thy people, whom thou broughtest up out of Egypt;</hi> but Moses humbly turns them back upon God again: "They are <hi type="italic">thy people,</hi> thou art their Lord and owner; I am but their servant. <hi type="italic">Thou broughtest them forth out of Egypt;</hi> I was but the instrument in thy hand; that was done in order to their deliverance which thou only couldest do." Though their being his people was a reason why he should be angry with them for setting up another god, yet it was a reason why he should not be so angry with them as to consume them. Nothing is more natural than for a father to correct his son, but nothing more unnatural than for a father to slay his son. And as the relation is a good plea ("they are <hi type="italic">thy people</hi>"), so is the experience they had had of his kindness to them: "Thou <hi type="italic">broughtest them out of Egypt,</hi> though they were unworthy, and had there served the gods of the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.15">Josh. xxiv. 15</reference>. If thou didst that for them, notwithstanding their sins in Egypt, wilt thou undo it for their sins of the same nature in the wilderness?" (2.) He pleads the concern of God's glory (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore should the Egyptians say, For mischief did he bring them out?</hi> Israel is dear to Moses as his kindred, as his charge; but it is the glory of God that he is most concerned for; this lies nearer his heart than any thing else. If Israel could perish without any reproach to God's name, Moses could persuade himself to sit down contented; but he cannot bear to hear God reflected on, and therefore this he insists upon, <hi type="italic">Lord, what will the Egyptians say?</hi> Their eyes, and the eyes of all the neighbouring nations, were now upon Israel; from the wondrous beginnings of that people, they raised their expectations of something great in their latter end; but, if a people so strangely saved should be suddenly ruined, what would the world say of it, especially the Egyptians, who have such an implacable hatred both to Israel and to the God of Israel? They would say, "God was either weak, and could not, or fickle, and would not, complete the salvation he began; he brought them forth to that mountain, not to sacrifice (as was pretended), but to be sacrificed." They will not consider the provocation given by Israel, to justify the proceeding, but will think it cause enough for triumph that God and his people could not agree, but that their God had done that which they (the Egyptians) wished to see done. Note, The glorifying of God's name, as it ought to be our first petition (it is so in the Lord's prayer), so it ought to be our great plea, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.9">Ps. lxxix. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Do not disgrace the throne of thy glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">Jer. xiv. 21</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Jer.33.8-Jer.33.9">Jer. xxxiii. 8, 9</reference>. And, if we would with comfort plead this with God as a reason why he should not destroy us, we ought to plead it with ourselves as a reason why we should not offend him: <hi type="italic">What will the Egyptians say?</hi> We ought always to be careful that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed through us. (3.) He pleads God's promise to the patriarchs that he would multiply their seed, and give them the land of Canaan for an inheritance, and this promise confirmed by an oath, an oath by himself, since he could swear by no greater, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.13">v. 13</reference>. God's promises are to be our pleas in prayer; for what he has promised he is able to perform, and the honour of this truth is engaged for the performance of it. "Lord, if Israel be cut off, what will become of the promise? Shall their unbelief make that of no effect? God forbid." Thus we must take our encouragement in prayer from God only. <div eID="gen2078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2079" type="x-p"/> IV. God graciously abated the rigour of the sentence, and <hi type="italic">repented of the evil he thought to do</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.14">v. 14</reference>); though he designed to punish them, yet he would not ruin them. See here, 1. The power of prayer; God suffers himself to be prevailed with by the humble believing importunity of intercessors. 2. The compassion of God towards poor sinners, and how ready he is to forgive. Thus he has given other proofs besides his own oath that he has no pleasure in the death of those that die; for he not only pardons upon the repentance of sinners, but spares and reprieves upon the intercession of others for them.
entries.1b917f2cd551cf6aeb7e4f074356cd5ac6e2dbaa: <div eID="gen2079" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Moses Breaks the Tablets of the Law. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2080" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Moses turned, and went down from the mount, and the two tables of the testimony <hi type="italic">were</hi> in his hand: the tables <hi type="italic">were</hi> written on both their sides; on the one side and on the other <hi type="italic">were</hi> they written. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the tables <hi type="italic">were</hi> the work of God, and the writing <hi type="italic">was</hi> the writing of God, graven upon the tables. <hi type="super">17</hi> And when Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said unto Moses, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a noise of war in the camp. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he said, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> not the voice of <hi type="italic">them that</hi> shout for mastery, neither <hi type="italic">is it</hi> the voice of <hi type="italic">them that</hi> cry for being overcome: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the noise of <hi type="italic">them that</hi> sing do I hear. <hi type="super">19</hi> And it came to pass, as soon as he came nigh unto the camp, that he saw the calf, and the dancing: and Moses' anger waxed hot, and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount. 20 And he took the calf which they had made, and burnt <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the fire, and ground <hi type="italic">it</hi> to powder, and strawed <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink <hi type="italic">of it.</hi> <div eID="gen2080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2081" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The favour of God to Moses, in trusting him with the two tables of the testimony, which, though of common stone, were far more valuable than all the precious stones that adorned the breast-plate of Aaron. The topaz of Ethiopia could not equal them, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.15-Exod.32.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. God himself, without the ministry either of man or angel (for aught that appears), wrote the ten commandments on these tables, <hi type="italic">on both their sides,</hi> some on one table and some on the other, so that they were folded together like a book, to be deposited in the ark. <div eID="gen2081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2082" type="x-p"/> II. The familiarity between Moses and Joshua. While Moses was in the cloud, as in the presence-chamber, Joshua continued as near as he might, in the anti-chamber (as it were), waiting till Moses came out, that he might be ready to attend him; and though he was all alone for forty days (fed, it is likely, with manna), yet he was not weary of waiting, as the people were, but when Moses came down he came with him, and not till then. And here we are told what constructions they put upon the noise that they heard in the camp, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.17-Exod.32.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. Though Moses had been so long in immediate converse with God, yet he did not disdain to talk freely with his servant Joshua. Those whom God advances he preserves from being puffed up. Nor did he disdain to talk of the affairs of the camp. Blessed Paul was not the less mindful of the church on earth for having been in the third heavens, where he heard unspeakable words. Joshua, who was a military man, and had the command of the train-bands, feared there was <hi type="italic">a noise of war in the camp,</hi> and then he would be missed; but Moses, having received notice of it from God, better distinguished the sound, and was aware that it was <hi type="italic">the voice of those that sing.</hi> It does not however appear that he told Joshua what he knew of the occasion of their singing; for we should not be forward to proclaim men's faults: they will be known too soon. <div eID="gen2082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2083" type="x-p"/> III. The great and just displeasure of Moses against Israel, for their idolatry. Knowing what to expect, he was presently aware of the golden calf, and the sport the people made with it. He saw how merry they could be in his absence, how soon he was forgotten among them, and what little thought they had of him and his return. He might justly take this ill, as an affront to himself, but this was the least part of the grievance; he resented it as an offence to God, and the scandal of his people. See what a change it is to come down from the mount of communion with God to converse with a world that <hi type="italic">lies in wickedness.</hi> In God we see nothing but what is pure and pleasant, in the world nothing but pollution and provocation. Moses was the meekest man on the earth, and yet when he saw <hi type="italic">the calf, and the dancing,</hi> his <hi type="italic">anger waxed hot.</hi> Note, It is no breach of the law of meekness to show our displeasure at the wickedness of the wicked. Those are <hi type="italic">angry and sin not</hi> that are angry at sin only, not as against themselves, but as against God. Ephesus is famous for patience, and yet <hi type="italic">cannot bear those that are evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.2">Rev. ii. 2</reference>. It becomes us to be cool in our own cause, but warm in God's. Moses showed himself very angry, both by breaking the tables and burning the calf, that he might, by these expressions of strong indignation, awaken the people to a sense of the greatness of the sin they had been guilty of, which they would have been ready to make light of if he had not thus shown his resentment, as one in earnest for their conviction. 1. To convince them that they had forfeited and lost the favour of God, <hi type="italic">he broke the tables,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.19">v. 19</reference>. Though God knew of their sin, before Moses came down, yet he did not order him to leave the tables behind him, but gave them to him to take down in his hand, that the people might see how forward God was to take them into covenant with himself, and that nothing but their own sin prevented it; yet he put in into his heart, when the iniquity of Ephraim was discovered (as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.1">Hos. vii. 1</reference>), to break the tables before their eyes (as it is <reference osisRef="Deut.9.17">Deut. ix. 17</reference>), that the sight of it might the more affect them, and fill them with confusion, when they saw what blessings they had lost. Thus, they being guilty of so notorious an infraction of the treaty now on foot, the writings were torn, even when they lay ready to be sealed. Note, The greatest sign of God's displeasure against any person or people is his taking his law from them. The breaking of the tables is the breaking of the <hi type="italic">staff of beauty and band</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.10">Zech. xi. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.14">14</reference>); it leaves a people unchurched and undone. Some think that Moses sinned in breaking the tables, and observe that, when men are angry, they are in danger of breaking all God's commandments; but it rather seems to be an act of justice than of passion, and we do not find that he himself speaks of it afterwards (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.17">Deut. ix. 17</reference>) with any regret. 2. To convince them that they had betaken themselves to a God that could not help them, he <hi type="italic">burnt the calf</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.20">v. 20</reference>), melted it down, and then filed it to dust; and, that the powder to which it was reduced might be taken notice of throughout the camp, he strewed it upon that water of which they all drank. That it might appear that <hi type="italic">an idol is nothing in the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1 Cor. viii. 4</reference>); he reduced this to atoms, that it might be as near nothing as could be. To show that false gods cannot help their worshippers, he here showed that this could not save itself, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1-Isa.46.2">Isa. xlvi. 1, 2</reference>. And to teach us that all the relics of idolatry ought to be abolished, and that the names of Baalim should be taken away, the very dust to which it was ground was scattered. Filings of gold are precious (we say), and therefore are carefully gathered up; but the filings of the golden calf were odious, and must be scattered with detestation. Thus the idols of silver and gold must be cast to the moles and the bats (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa. ii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">xxx. 22</reference>), and Ephraim shall say, <hi type="italic">What have I to do any more with idols?</hi> His mixing this powder with their drink signified to them that the curse they had thereby brought upon themselves would mingle itself with all their enjoyments, and embitter them; it would enter into their bowels like water, and like oil into their bones. <hi type="italic">The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways;</hi> he shall drink as he brews. These were indeed waters of Marah.
entries.8b1c33737d0e45bd29cb89f7d6890813f7a3e1e3: <div eID="gen2083" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Moses Reproves Aaron; Destruction of the Idolaters. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2084" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And Moses said unto Aaron, What did this people unto thee, that thou hast brought so great a sin upon them? 22 And Aaron said, Let not the anger of my lord wax hot: thou knowest the people, that they <hi type="italic">are set</hi> on mischief. 23 For they said unto me, Make us gods, which shall go before us: for <hi type="italic">as for</hi> this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him. <hi type="super">24</hi> And I said unto them, Whosoever hath any gold, let them break <hi type="italic">it</hi> off. So they gave <hi type="italic">it</hi> me: then I cast it into the fire, and there came out this calf. <hi type="super">25</hi> And when Moses saw that the people <hi type="italic">were</hi> naked; (for Aaron had made them naked unto <hi type="italic">their</hi> shame among their enemies:) <hi type="super">26</hi> Then Moses stood in the gate of the camp, and said, Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's side? <hi type="italic">let him come</hi> unto me. And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves together unto him. 27 And he said unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, Put every man his sword by his side, <hi type="italic">and</hi> go in and out from gate to gate throughout the camp, and slay every man his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbour. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the children of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. <hi type="super">29</hi> For Moses had said, Consecrate yourselves to day to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , even every man upon his son, and upon his brother; that he may bestow upon you a blessing this day. <div eID="gen2084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2085" type="x-p"/> Moses, having shown his just indignation against the sin of Israel by breaking the tables and burning the calf, now proceeds to reckon with the sinners and to call them to an account, herein acting as the representative of God, who is not only a holy God, and hates sin, but a just God, and is engaged in honour to punish it, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.18">Isa. lix. 18</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen2085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2086" type="x-p"/> I. He begins with Aaron, as God began with Adam, because he was the principal person, though not first in the transgression, but drawn into it. Observe here, <div eID="gen2086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2087" type="x-p"/> 1. The just reproof Moses gives him, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.21">v. 21</reference>. He does not order him to be cut-off, as those (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.27">v. 27</reference>) that had been the ring-leaders in the sin. Note, A great deal of difference will be made between those that presumptuously rush into sin and those that through infirmity are surprised into it, between those that overtake the fault that flees from them and those that are overtaken in the fault they flee from. See <reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal. vi. 1</reference>. Not but that Aaron deserved to be cut off for this sin, and would have been so if Moses had not interceded particularly for him, as appears <reference osisRef="Deut.9.20">Deut. ix. 20</reference>. And having prevailed with God for him, to save him from ruin, he here expostulates with him, to bring him to repentance. He puts Aaron upon considering, (1.) What he had done to this people: <hi type="italic">Thou hast brought so great a sin upon them.</hi> The sin of idolatry is a great sin, so great a sin that the evil of it cannot be expressed; the people, as the first movers, might be said to bring the sin upon Aaron; but he being a magistrate, who should have suppressed it, and yet aiding and abetting it, might truly be said to bring it upon them, because he hardened their hearts and strengthened their hands in it. It is a shocking thing for governors to humour people in their sins, and give countenance to that to which they should be a terror. Observe, in general, Those who bring sin upon others, either by drawing them into it or encouraging them in it, do more mischief than they are aware of; we really hate those whom we either bring or suffer sin upon, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev. xix. 17</reference>. Those that share in sin help to break their partners, and really ruin one another. (2.) What moved him to it: <hi type="italic">What did this people unto thee?</hi> He takes it for granted that it must needs be something more than ordinary that prevailed with Aaron to do such a thing, thus insinuating an excuse for him, because he knew that his heart was upright: "<hi type="italic">What did they?</hi> Did they accost thee fairly, and wheedle thee into it; and durst thou displease thy God, to please the people? Did they overcome thee by importunity; and hadst thou so little resolution left as to yield to the stream of a popular clamour? Did they threaten to stone thee; and couldest not thou have opposed God's threatenings to theirs, and frightened them worse than they could frighten thee?" Note, We must never be drawn into sin by any thing that man can say or do to us, for it will not justify us to say that we were so drawn in. Men can but tempt us to sin; they cannot force us. Men can but frighten us; if we do not comply, they cannot hurt us. <div eID="gen2087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2088" type="x-p"/> 2. The frivolous excuse Aaron makes for himself. We will hope that he testified his repentance for the sin afterwards better than he did now; for what he says here has little in it of the language of a penitent. If a just man fall, he shall rise again, but perhaps not quickly. (1.) He deprecates the anger of Moses only, whereas he should have deprecated God's anger in the first place: <hi type="italic">Let not the anger of my Lord wax hot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.22">v. 22</reference>. (2.) He lays all the fault upon the people: <hi type="italic">They are set on mischief, and they said, Make us gods.</hi> It is natural to us to endeavour thus to transfer our guilt; we have it in our kind, Adam and Eve did so; sin is a brat that nobody is willing to own. Aaron was now the chief magistrate and had power over the people, and yet pleads that the people overpowered him; he that had authority to restrain them, yet had so little resolution as to yield to them. (3.) It is well if he did not intend a reflection upon Moses, as accessory to the sin, by staying so long on the mount, in repeating, without need, that invidious surmise of the people, <hi type="italic">As for this Moses, we know not what has become of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.23">v. 23</reference>. (4.) He extenuates and conceals his own share in the sin, as if he had only bidden them <hi type="italic">break off their gold</hi> that they had about them, intending to make a hasty assay for the present, and to try what he could make of the gold that was next hand: and childishly insinuates that when he cast the gold into the fire it came out, either by accident or by the magic art of some of the mixed multitude (as the Jewish writers dream), in this shape; but not a word of his graving and fashioning it, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.24">v. 24</reference>. But Moses relates to all ages what he did (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.4">v. 4</reference>), though he himself here would not own it. Note, <hi type="italic">He that covers his sin shall not prosper,</hi> for sooner or later it will be discovered. Well, this was all Aaron had to say for himself; and he had better have said nothing, for his defence did but aggravate his offence; and yet he is not only spared, but preferred; as sin did abound, grace did much more abound. <div eID="gen2088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2089" type="x-p"/> II. The people are next to be judged for this sin. The approach of Moses soon spoiled their sport and turned their dancing into trembling. Those that hectored Aaron into a compliance with them in their sin durst not look Moses in the face, nor make the least opposition to the severity which he thought fit to use both against the idol and against the idolaters. Note, It is not impossible to make those sins which were committed with daring presumption appear contemptible, when the insolent perpetrators of them slink away overwhelmed in their own confusion. <hi type="italic">The king that sits upon the throne of judgment scatters away all evil with his eyes.</hi> Observe two things:— <div eID="gen2089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2090" type="x-p"/> 1. How they were exposed to shame by their sin: <hi type="italic">The people were naked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.25">v. 25</reference>), not so much because they had some of them lost their ear-rings (that was inconsiderable), but because they had lost their integrity, and lay under the reproach of ingratitude to their best benefactor, and a treacherous revolt from their rightful Lord. It was a shame to them, and a perpetual blot, that they <hi type="italic">changed their glory into the similitude of an ox.</hi> Other nations boasted that they were true to their false gods; well may Israel blush for being false to the true God. Thus were they <hi type="italic">made naked,</hi> stripped of their ornaments, and exposed to contempt; stripped of their armour, and liable to insults. Thus our first parents, when they had sinned, became <hi type="italic">naked, to their shame.</hi> Note, Those that do dishonour to God really bring the greatest dishonour upon themselves: so Israel here did, and Moses was concerned to see it, though they themselves were not; he <hi type="italic">saw that they were naked.</hi> <div eID="gen2090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2091" type="x-p"/> 2. The course that Moses took to roll away this reproach, not by concealing the sin, or putting any false colour upon it, but by punishing it, and so bearing a public testimony against it. Whenever it should be case in their teeth that they had <hi type="italic">made a calf in Horeb,</hi> they might have this to say, in answer to those that reproached them, that though it was true there were those that did so, yet justice was executed upon them. The government disallowed the sin, and suffered not the sinners to go unpunished. They did so, but they paid dearly for it. Thus (said God) thou shalt <hi type="italic">put the evil away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.13.5">Deut. xiii. 5</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen2091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2092" type="x-p"/> (1.) By whom vengeance was taken—by the children of Levi (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.26">v. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.28">28</reference>); not by the immediate hand of God himself, as on Nadab and Abihu, but by the sword of man, to teach them that idolatry was an <hi type="italic">iniquity to be punished by the judge,</hi> being a <hi type="italic">denial of the God that is above,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.28">Job xxxi. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.13.9">Deut. xiii. 9</reference>. It was to be done by the sword of their own brethren, that the execution of justice might redound more to the honour of the nation. And, if they must fall now into the hands of man, better so than flee before their enemies. The innocent must be culled out to be the executioners of the guilty, that it might be the more effectual warning to themselves, that they did not the like another time; and the putting of them upon such an unpleasant service, and so much against the grain as this must needs be, to kill their next neighbours, was a punishment to them too for not appearing sooner to prevent the sin, and make head against it. The Levites particularly were employed in doing this execution; for, it should seem, there were more of them than of any other tribe that had kept themselves free from the contagion, which was the more laudable because Aaron, the head of their tribe, was so deeply concerned in it. Now here we are told, [1.] How the Levites were called out to this service: <hi type="italic">Moses stood in the gate of the camp,</hi> the place of judgment; there he <hi type="italic">displayed a banner,</hi> as it were, because of the truth, to enlist soldiers for God. He proclaimed, <hi type="italic">Who is on the Lord's side?</hi> The idolaters had set up the golden calf for their standard, and now Moses set up his, in opposition to them. Now <hi type="italic">Moses clad himself with zeal</hi> as with a robe, and summoned all those to appear forthwith that were on God's side, against the golden calf. He does not proclaim, as Jehu, "<hi type="italic">Who is on my side</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.32">2 Kings ix. 32</reference>), to avenge the indignity done to me?" but, <hi type="italic">Who is on the Lord's side?</hi> It was God's cause that he espoused <hi type="italic">against the evil-doers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">Ps. xciv. 16</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There are two great interests on foot in the world, with the one or the other of which all the children of men are siding. The interest of sin and wickedness is the devil's interest, and all wicked people side with that interest; the interest of truth and holiness is God's interest, with which all godly people side; and it is a case that will not admit a neutrality. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It concerns us all to enquire whether we are on the Lord's side or not. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Those who are on his side are comparatively but few, and sometimes seem fewer than really they are. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> God does sometimes call out those that are on his side to appear for him, as witnesses, as soldiers, as intercessors. [2.] How they were commissioned for this service (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Slay every man his brother,</hi> that is, "Slay all those that you know to have been active for the making and worshipping of the golden calf, though they were your own nearest relations, or dearest friends." The crime was committed publicly, the Levites saw who of their acquaintance were concerned in it, and therefore needed no other direction than their own knowledge whom to slay. And probably the greatest part of those that were guilty were known, and known to be so, by some or other of the Levites who were employed in the execution. Yet, it should seem, they were to slay those only whom they found <hi type="italic">abroad in the streets</hi> of the camp; for it might be hoped that those who had retired into their tents were ashamed of what they had done, and were upon their knees, repenting. Those are marked for ruin who persist in sin, and are not ashamed of the abominations they have committed, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.12">Jer. viii. 12</reference>. But how durst the Levites encounter so great a body, who probably were much enraged by the burning of their calf? It is easy to account for this; a sense of guilt disheartened the delinquents, and a divine commission animated the executioners. And one thing that put life into them was that Moses had said, <hi type="italic">Consecrate yourselves to day to the Lord, that he may bestow a blessing upon you,</hi> thereby intimating to them that they now stood fair for preferment and that, if they would but signalize themselves upon this occasion, it would be construed into such a consecration of themselves to God, and to his service, as would put upon their tribe a perpetual honour. Those that consecrate themselves to the Lord he will set apart for himself. Those that do the duty shall have the dignity; and, if we do signal services for God, he will bestow especial blessings upon us. There was a blessing designed for the tribe of Levi; now says Moses, "<hi type="italic">Consecrate yourselves to the Lord,</hi> that you may qualify yourselves to receive the blessing." The Levites were to assist in the offering of sacrifice to God; and now they must begin with the offering of these sacrifices to the honour of divine justice. Those that are to minister about holy things must be not only sincere and serious, but warm and zealous, bold and courageous, for God and godliness. Thus all Christians, but especially ministers, must <hi type="italic">forsake father and mother,</hi> and prefer the service of Christ and his interest far before their nearest and dearest relations; for if we love our relations better than Christ we are not <hi type="italic">worthy of him.</hi> See how this zeal of the Levites is applauded, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen2092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2093" type="x-p"/> (2.) On whom vengeance is taken: <hi type="italic">There fell of the people that day about 3000 men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.28">v. 28</reference>. Probably these were but few, in comparison with the many that were guilty; but these were the men that headed the rebellion, and were therefore picked out, to be made examples of, for terror to all others. Those that in the morning were shouting and dancing before night were dying in their own blood; such a sudden change do the judgments of God sometimes make with sinners that are secure and jovial in their sin, as with Belshazzar by the hand-writing upon the wall. This is written for warning to us. <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.7">1 Cor. x. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">Neither be you idolaters, as were some of them.</hi>
entries.4d3d645d6eaf5f93646aa4d4430f236731c26226: <div eID="gen2093" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Intercession of Moses. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2094" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> And it came to pass on the morrow, that Moses said unto the people, Ye have sinned a great sin: and now I will go up unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; peradventure I shall make an atonement for your sin. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Moses returned unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made them gods of gold. 32 Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin—; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written. 33 And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book. <hi type="super">34</hi> Therefore now go, lead the people unto <hi type="italic">the place</hi> of which I have spoken unto thee: behold, mine Angel shall go before thee: nevertheless in the day when I visit I will visit their sin upon them. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> plagued the people, because they made the calf, which Aaron made. <div eID="gen2094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2095" type="x-p"/> Moses, having executed justice upon the principal offenders, is here dealing both with the people and with God. <div eID="gen2095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2096" type="x-p"/> I. With the people, to bring them to repentance, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.30">v. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen2096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2097" type="x-p"/> 1. When some were slain, lest the rest should imagine that, because they were exempt from the capital punishment, they were therefore looked upon as free from guilt, Moses here tells the survivors, <hi type="italic">You have sinned a great sin,</hi> and therefore, though you have escaped this time, <hi type="italic">except you repent, you shall all likewise perish.</hi> That they might not think lightly of the sin itself, he calls it <hi type="italic">a great sin;</hi> and that they might not think themselves innocent, because perhaps they were not all so deeply guilty as some of those that were put to death, he tells them all, <hi type="italic">You have sinned a great sin.</hi> The work of ministers is to show people their sins, and the greatness of their sins. "<hi type="italic">You have sinned,</hi> and therefore you are undone if your sins be not pardoned, for ever undone without a Saviour. It is a great sin, and therefore calls for great sorrow, for it puts you in great danger." To affect them with the greatness of their sin he intimates to them what a difficult thing it would be to make up the quarrel which God had with them for it. (1.) It would not be done, unless he himself <hi type="italic">went up unto the Lord</hi> on purpose, and gave as long and as solemn attendance as he had done for the receiving of the law. And yet, (2.) Even so it was but a peradventure that he should make atonement for them; the case was extremely hazardous. This should convince us of the great evil there is in sin, that he who undertook to make atonement found it no easy thing to do it; he must <hi type="italic">go up to the Lord</hi> with his own blood to <hi type="italic">make atonement.</hi> The malignity of sin appears in the price of pardons. <div eID="gen2097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2098" type="x-p"/> 2. Yet it was some encouragement to the people (when they were told that they had <hi type="italic">sinned a great sin</hi>) to hear that Moses, who had so great an interest in heaven and so true an affection for them, would <hi type="italic">go up unto the Lord to make atonement</hi> for them. Consolation should go along with conviction: first wound, and then heal; first show people the greatness of their sin, and then make known to them the atonement, and give them hopes of mercy. <hi type="italic">Moses will go up unto the Lord,</hi> though it be but a <hi type="italic">peradventure</hi> that he should make atonement. Christ, the great Mediator, went upon greater certainty than this, for he had lain in the bosom of the Father, and perfectly knew all his counsels. But to us poor supplicants it is encouragement enough in prayer for particular mercies that <hi type="italic">peradventure</hi> we may obtain them, though we have not an absolute promise. <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.3">Zeph. ii. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">It may be, you shall be hid.</hi> In our prayers for others, we should be humbly earnest with God, though it is but a <hi type="italic">peradventure that God will give them repentance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2 Tim. ii. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen2098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2099" type="x-p"/> II. He intercedes with God for mercy. Observe, <div eID="gen2099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2100" type="x-p"/> 1. How pathetic his address was. <hi type="italic">Moses returned unto the Lord,</hi> not to receive further instructions about the tabernacle: there were no more conferences now about that matter. Thus men's sins and follies make work for their friends and ministers, unpleasant work, many times, and give great interruptions to that work which they delight in. Moses in this address expresses, (1.) His great detestation of the people's sin, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.31">v. 31</reference>. He speaks as one overwhelmed with the horror of it: <hi type="italic">Oh! this people have sinned a great sin.</hi> God had first told him of it (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.7">v. 7</reference>), and now he tells God of it, by way of lamentation. He does not call them God's people, he knew they were unworthy to be called so; but this people, this treacherous ungrateful people, they have made for themselves gods of gold. It is a great sin indeed to make gold our god, as those do that make it their hope, and set their heart on it. He does not go about to excuse or extenuate the sin; but what he had said to them by way of conviction he says to God by way of confession: <hi type="italic">They have sinned a great sin;</hi> he came not to make apologies, but to make atonement. "Lord, pardon the sin, <hi type="italic">for it is great,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">Ps. xxv. 11</reference>. (2.) His great desire of the people's welfare (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet now</hi> it is not too great a sin for infinite mercy to pardon, and therefore <hi type="italic">if thou wilt forgive their sin.</hi> What then Moses? It is an abrupt expression, "<hi type="italic">If thou wilt,</hi> I desire no more; <hi type="italic">if thou wilt,</hi> thou wilt be praised, I shall be pleased, and abundantly recompensed for my intercession." It is an expression like that of the dresser of the vineyard (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.9">Luke xiii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">If it bear fruit;</hi> or, <hi type="italic">If thou wilt forgive,</hi> is as much as, "O that thou wouldest forgive!" as <reference osisRef="Luke.19.42">Luke xix. 42</reference>, <hi type="italic">If thou hadst known</hi> is, <hi type="italic">O that thou hadst known.</hi> "But <hi type="italic">if not,</hi> if the decree has gone forth, and there is no remedy, but they must be ruined; if this punishment which has already been inflicted on many is not sufficient (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.6">2 Cor. ii. 6</reference>), but they must all be cut off, <hi type="italic">blot me, I pray thee, out of the book which thou hast written;</hi>" that is, "If they must be cut off, let me be cut off with them, and cut short of Canaan; if all Israel must perish, I am content to perish with them; let not the land of promise be mine by survivorship." This expression may be illustrated from <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.9">Ezek. xiii. 9</reference>, where this is threatened against the false prophets, <hi type="italic">They shall not be written in the writing of the house of Israel, neither shall they enter into the land of Israel.</hi> God had told Moses that, if he would not interpose he would make of him a <hi type="italic">great nation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">v. 10</reference>. "No," says Moses, "I am so far from desiring to see my name and family built up on the ruins of Israel, that I will choose rather to sink with them. If I cannot prevent their destruction, let me not see it (<reference osisRef="Num.11.15">Num. xi. 15</reference>); let me not be <hi type="italic">written among the living</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">Isa. iv. 3</reference>), nor among those that are marked for preservation; even let me die in the last ditch." Thus he expresses his tender affection for the people, and is a type of the good Shepherd, that <hi type="italic">lays down his life for the sheep</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.11">John x. 11</reference>), who was to be <hi type="italic">cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of my people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">Isa. liii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>. He is also an example of public-spiritedness to all, especially to those in public stations. All private interests must be made subordinate to the good and welfare of communities. It is no great matter what becomes of us and our families in this world, so that it go well with the church of God, and there be peace upon Israel. Moses thus importunes for a pardon, and wrestles with God, not prescribing to him ("If thou wilt not forgive, thou art either unjust or unkind"); no, he is far from that; but, "If not, let me die with the Israelites, and the will of the Lord be done." <div eID="gen2100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2101" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe how prevalent his address was. God would not take him at his word; no, he will not blot any out of his book but those that by their wilful disobedience have forfeited the honour of being enrolled in it (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.33">v. 33</reference>); the soul that sins shall die, and not the innocent for the guilty. This was also an intimation of mercy to the people, that they should not all be destroyed in a body, but those only that had a hand in the sin. Thus Moses gets ground by degrees. God would not at first give him full assurances of his being reconciled to them, lest, if the comfort of a pardon were too easily obtained, they should be emboldened to do the like again, and should not be made sensible enough of the evil of the sin. Comforts are suspended that convictions may be the deeper impressed: also God would hereby exercise the faith and zeal of Moses, their great intercessor. Further, in answer to the address of Moses, (1.) God promises, notwithstanding this, to go on with his kind intention of giving them the land of Canaan, the land he had <hi type="italic">spoken to them of,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.34">v. 34</reference>. Therefore he sends Moses back to them to lead them, though they were unworthy of him, and promises that his angel should go before them, some created angel that was employed in the common services of the kingdom of providence, which intimated that they were not to expect any thing for the future to be done for them out of the common road of providence, not any thing extraordinary. Moses afterwards obtained a promise of God's special presence with them (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.14">ch. xxxiii. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.17">17</reference>); but at present this was all he could prevail for. (2.) Yet he threatens to remember this sin against them when hereafter he should see cause to punish them for other sins: "<hi type="italic">When I visit, I will visit</hi> for this among the rest. Next time I take the rod in hand, they shall have one stripe the more for this." The Jews have a saying, grounded on this, that henceforward no judgment fell upon Israel but there was in it an ounce of the powder of the golden calf. I see no ground in scripture for the opinion some are of, that God would not have burdened them with such a multitude of sacrifices and other ceremonial institutions if they had not provoked him by worshipping the golden calf. On the contrary, Stephen says that when they <hi type="italic">made a calf, and offered sacrifice to the idol, God turned, and gave them up to worship the host of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.41-Acts.7.42">Acts vii. 41, 42</reference>); so that the strange addictedness of that people to the sin of idolatry was a just judgment upon them for making and worshipping the golden calf, and a judgment they were never quite freed from till the captivity of Babylon. See <reference osisRef="Rom.1.23-Rom.1.25">Rom. i. 23-25</reference>. Note, Many that are not immediately cut off in their sins are reserved for a further day of reckoning: vengeance is slow, but sure. For the present, <hi type="italic">the Lord plagued the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.35">v. 35</reference>), probably by the pestilence, or some other infectious disease, which was a messenger of God's wrath, and an earnest of worse. Aaron made the calf, and yet it is said the people made it, because they worshipped it. <hi type="italic">Deos qui rogat, ille facit—He who asks for gods makes them.</hi> Aaron was not plagued, but the people; for his was a sin of infirmity, theirs a presumptuous sin, between which there is a great difference, not always discernable to us, but evident to God, whose judgment therefore, we are sure, is according to truth. Thus Moses prevailed for a reprieve and a mitigation of the punishment, but could not wholly turn away the wrath of God. This (some think) bespeaks the inability of the law of Moses to reconcile men to God and to perfect our peace with him, which was reserved for Christ to do, in whom alone it is that God so pardons sin as to <hi type="italic">remember it no more.</hi>  <chapter eID="Exod.32"/> <div eID="gen2101" type="x-p"/>

entries.7567c9788c8e2de8aaba80922595de9d939b2791: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv907"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 32</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.32.1-Exod.32.35">Ex 32:1-35</reference>. The Golden Calf.</title> <div sID="gen1264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv907"/><hi type="bold">1. when the people saw that Moses delayed--</hi>They supposed that he had lost his way in the darkness or perished in the fire.<div eID="gen1264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron--</hi>rather, "against" Aaron in a tumultuous manner, to compel him to do what they wished. The incidents related in this chapter disclose a state of popular sentiment and feeling among the Israelites that stands in singular contrast to the tone of profound and humble reverence they displayed at the giving of the law. Within a space of little more than thirty days, their impressions were dissipated.
